title: Letter by letter
hook: spelling a name, you go letter by letter; do each duty in order (Meditations 6.26)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Rusticus, the teacher behind an emperor's offer: show me I'm wrong, and I'll gladly change. Your line was show me.

You're on the phone with customer service, spelling your last name. The agent gets it wrong. You spell it again, slowly. Wrong again, a different letter this time. Now there's a little heat in your voice, and the letters come out louder, as if volume could fix it. Marcus Aurelius uses this very moment, spelling a name aloud, as a picture for getting through a whole day's work.

In Meditations six, twenty-six, Marcus says: suppose someone asks you how to write the name Antoninus. That was the name of his adoptive father. Do you shout each letter at him? And if he gets angry, do you get angry back? No. You go on calmly, counting off the letters one at a time. So it is in life, he says. Every duty is made up of certain parts, the way a name is made of letters. Notice them, and do them in order. Then the part about anger: keep going without being disturbed, and without showing anger toward people who are angry with you. That's the phone call. Their frustration doesn't change the next letter. You still say N, then T, then O. Getting louder just adds another angry person to the line. Why it works: a whole duty, a tax return, a hard conversation, a move, can feel huge and blurry. Broken into letters, each piece is small enough to say clearly. And there's an odd calm in it. When you're on T, you don't have to be on S. You just have to say T well. Marcus isn't describing a productivity trick. He's describing a temper: the person who goes letter by letter is less likely to lose their head, because they always know exactly what comes next.
screen: `HOW DO YOU SPELL ANTONINUS?` · `EVERY DUTY HAS ITS LETTERS.` · `DON'T SHOUT BACK.` · `ONE LETTER IS SMALL ENOUGH.` · then, large: `LETTER BY LETTER.`

segments.voice: Choose one task waiting for you that feels too big or tangled, and break it into letters: the very first piece, the second, the third. Name them slowly, without doing them yet, like letters in a name. Then come back to the breath, one at a time, in and out.
Antoninus, the name Marcus imagined spelling calmly, letter by letter, even if the person asking grew impatient. Today's word.
Your line: one letter at a time. A whole duty is just its letters, said in order. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 580 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SEEN THE PRESENT, SEEN ALL.`

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes use 'letter by letter' for large or stressful work: breaking a duty into its parts and doing each in order, without matching the impatience of people around them.
